Chapter 7
Concerning New Principalities Which Are Acquired Either By The Arms Of Others Or By Good Fortune

Private citizens who become princes entirely through Fortuna have an easy time rising, but a very hard time staying on top. They face no hurdles on the way up because they practically fly. The real difficulties hit them once they reach the summit. This happens to people who buy a state or receive it as a favor. Think of the many princes Darius installed in Greece, across the cities of Ionia and the Hellespont. He made them rulers simply to hold those cities for his own security and glory. The same goes for the Roman emperors who went from common citizens to rulers by bribing the military.

These leaders rely entirely on the goodwill and the Fortuna of whoever put them in power. Both of those things are incredibly unstable and unreliable. Such rulers also lack the knowledge needed for the job. Unless they are men of immense ability and Virtù, you cannot expect someone who has only ever lived as a private citizen to know how to command. Furthermore, they cannot hold onto power because they do not have loyal and friendly armies of their own.

States that emerge overnight are just like anything else in nature that grows too fast. They simply cannot develop the deep roots and strong foundations needed to survive the first political storm. They will be overthrown. The only exception is if these unexpected princes have so much Virtù that they instantly figure out how to defend what Fortuna just tossed into their laps. They must quickly build the foundations after taking power, rather than building them beforehand like everyone else.

Let me give you two examples from recent memory about these two ways of becoming a prince, either by Virtù or by Fortuna. The examples are Francesco Sforza and Cesare Borgia. Francesco used the right methods and immense Virtù to rise from a private citizen to the Duke of Milan. Because he pushed through a thousand anxieties to get that power, he held onto it with very little trouble. On the other hand, Cesare Borgia, who the people called Duke Valentino, acquired his state through the political rise of his father, Pope Alexander the Sixth. When his father's power declined, Cesare lost his state. He lost it despite doing absolutely everything a wise and capable man should do. He took every possible measure to plant strong roots in the territories that the weapons and Fortuna of others had handed to him.

As I mentioned earlier, if you do not lay your foundations first, a man of incredible Virtù might still manage to lay them later. However, doing so is extremely difficult for the architect and dangerous for the entire building. If you look at every step Cesare Borgia took, you will see that he built solid foundations for his future power. I do not think it is a waste of time to discuss them. In fact, I do not know any better advice to give a new prince than the example of Borgia's actions. If his plans eventually failed, it was not his fault. He was simply crushed by the extraordinary and extreme malice of Fortuna.

When Pope Alexander the Sixth wanted to make his son, the Duke, powerful, he faced many immediate and future problems. First, he saw no way to give his son a state unless it belonged to the Church. But if he tried to steal from the Church, he knew the Duke of Milan and the Venetians would stop him. Faenza and Rimini were already under Venetian protection. On top of this, the military forces of Italy that he could have used were controlled by men who feared a powerful Pope. Specifically, the Orsini family, the Colonna family, and their followers held all the military cards.

Therefore, the Pope had to completely flip the board. He needed to throw the Italian powers into chaos so he could safely grab a piece of their territories. This turned out to be easy. He saw that the Venetians, for their own reasons, were already planning to bring the French back into Italy. The Pope did not try to stop this. Instead, he made it easier by officially dissolving the previous marriage of King Louis of France.

So, King Louis marched into Italy with Venetian help and the Pope's blessing. As soon as the King reached Milan, the Pope borrowed French soldiers to attack the Romagna region. The Romagna quickly surrendered out of fear of the French King's reputation. At this point, Cesare Borgia had conquered the Romagna and crushed the Colonna family. He wanted to secure his new land and conquer even more, but two things stood in his way. First, his own army did not seem loyal. Second, he could not trust the goodwill of France.

Borgia was relying on mercenary troops from the Orsini family, and he worried they would abandon him. He feared they would not only stop him from conquering more, but actually steal what he had already won. He worried the French King might do exactly the same thing. Borgia got a warning about the Orsini troops when he attacked Bologna after taking Faenza. He noticed the Orsini mercenaries marched into battle with extreme reluctance. As for the French King, Borgia learned his true intentions right after conquering the Duchy of Urbino. When Borgia launched an attack on Tuscany, the King forced him to stop. Right then and there, the Duke decided to never again rely on the weapons or the Fortuna of other men.

The first thing he did was weaken the Orsini and Colonna factions in Rome. He did this by poaching all their noble followers. He made these nobles his own men, gave them excellent pay, and honored them with high offices and commands based on their rank. Within a few months, their old loyalty to their factions completely vanished, replaced by total devotion to the Duke. After successfully scattering the Colonna family's followers, Borgia waited patiently for a chance to crush the Orsini family. That opportunity came quickly, and he played it perfectly.

The Orsini finally realized that the growing power of the Duke and the Church would mean their ultimate ruin. They called a secret meeting at Magione in Perugia. This meeting sparked a rebellion in Urbino, riots in the Romagna, and endless dangers for the Duke. He managed to crush all these threats with the help of the French. But once his authority was restored, he refused to risk everything by relying on the French or any other outside army again. Instead, he turned to deception.

Borgia was a master at hiding his true intentions. He used Signor Pagolo to broker a peace with the Orsini. The Duke showered Pagolo with money, fine clothes, and horses to win his trust. The Orsini were foolishly convinced by this performance and agreed to a reconciliation. Their gullibility led them right into Borgia's trap at Sinigalia. The Duke ruthlessly exterminated the Orsini leaders and turned their surviving followers into his own loyal allies. By doing this, Borgia built incredibly strong foundations for his power. He now controlled the entire Romagna and the Duchy of Urbino. Even better, the local people started to taste the prosperity he brought them, and they completely rallied to his side. Because this specific strategy is brilliant and should be copied by others, I must explain exactly how he did it.

When the Duke first took over the Romagna, he found it had been governed by weak, pathetic lords. These lords had robbed their subjects instead of ruling them. They caused division rather than unity, leaving the entire region overrun with theft, gang violence, and lawlessness. Borgia knew that to bring peace and enforce obedience, he needed to install a brutal, effective governor. So, he gave absolute power to Ramiro d’Orco, a swift and famously cruel man.

In a very short time, Ramiro crushed the criminals and restored complete peace and unity, gaining massive success. But then the Duke realized that giving someone such absolute, brutal authority was becoming dangerous. He knew the people were starting to hate Ramiro's extreme methods, and that hatred could blow back on him. To fix this, Borgia established a civil court in the center of the province, led by an excellent judge, where every city had its own lawyer.

The Duke knew the recent violence had sparked some resentment toward himself. He wanted to clear his name, wipe away the anger, and win the people over entirely. He needed to prove that any cruelty that had happened was not his fault, but simply the vicious nature of his minister. He used this as an excuse to act. One morning in the public square at Cesena, Borgia had Ramiro chopped in half. He left the bloody corpse in the piazza with a wooden chopping block and a bloody knife right beside it. The sheer barbaric shock of this gruesome spectacle left the people simultaneously satisfied and completely terrified.

But let us get back to the main point. The Duke was now highly powerful. He had secured himself against immediate threats by building his own loyal army and crushing all neighboring forces that could hurt him. Now, to continue his conquests, he had to deal with France. He knew the French King had realized his own mistake too late and would no longer support him. So, Borgia started hunting for new alliances. He began stalling the French while they marched toward Naples to fight the Spanish army besieging Gaeta. Borgia's goal was to lock down his defenses against the French. He would have easily pulled this off if Pope Alexander had lived.

That was how he handled the present. But looking to the future, Borgia had one massive fear. He worried that the next Pope might be an enemy who would try to steal back everything his father had given him. To prevent this, he executed a four-part strategy. First, he decided to completely wipe out the bloodlines of all the lords he had overthrown, leaving the new Pope with no excuse to restore them. Second, he bribed and won over all the Roman nobility, planning to use them to keep the new Pope in check. Third, he manipulated the College of Cardinals, packing it with his own loyal allies. Fourth, he aimed to grab so much power before his father died that he could survive the initial shock of a new Pope all on his own.

When Pope Alexander suddenly died, Borgia had successfully completed three of these four goals. He had butchered nearly every dispossessed lord he could catch, and very few escaped. He had the Roman nobles in his pocket. And he controlled the largest voting bloc in the College of Cardinals. As for expanding his power, he was on the verge of becoming the absolute master of Tuscany. He already owned Perugia and Piombino, and he had placed Pisa under his protection. The French had just been kicked out of Naples by the Spanish, meaning both sides now desperately needed Borgia's favor. So, with no need to worry about France anymore, he struck directly at Pisa.

Immediately after that, Lucca and Siena surrendered to him, driven partly by fear and partly by their hatred for the Florentines. Florence was left completely defenseless. If Borgia had just kept winning the way he was in the year his father died, he would have gained so much sheer power and reputation that he could have stood completely alone. He would never again need to rely on the armies or the Fortuna of other men, but solely on his own Virtù and strength.

But Pope Alexander died just five years after Borgia first drew his sword. The Pope left his son with only the Romagna fully secured. Everything else was up in the air. Worse, Borgia found himself trapped between two massively powerful, hostile armies, and he himself was deathly ill. Yet, the Duke possessed such ruthless boldness and extreme Virtù. He understood perfectly how men are won over or destroyed, and the foundations he built in such a short time were incredibly strong. If he had not had those two foreign armies breathing down his neck, or if he had just been healthy, he would have survived everything.

You can see how strong his foundations were. The entire Romagna waited loyally for him for over a month. Even though he was half-dead in Rome, he was perfectly safe. His old enemies, like the Baglioni, the Vitelli, and the Orsini, flooded into the city but could not lay a finger on him. He might not have been able to make his own chosen candidate Pope, but he had enough power to ensure his enemies were blocked from the throne. If he had only been in good health when his father died, he would have easily managed the whole crisis. On the very day Pope Julius the Second was elected, Borgia told me personally that he had planned for every possible scenario regarding his father's death. He had a countermove ready for everything. The one thing he never imagined was that, when his father finally died, he would be on his own deathbed.

When I look back at everything the Duke did, I cannot find a single flaw to blame him for. In fact, as I said before, I believe his life is the ultimate blueprint. He should be imitated by anyone who rises to power through the weapons or the Fortuna of others. Borgia had a relentless spirit and massive ambitions. He could not have played his hand any better. The only things that destroyed his grand designs were his father's sudden death and his own fatal sickness.

Therefore, if you are a new prince and you need to secure your state, win friends, and conquer enemies by force or fraud, look to him. If you need to make yourself loved and terrified by your people, and respected and followed by your soldiers, look to him. If you must exterminate those who have the power or the motive to hurt you, if you need to tear down the old system and replace it with a new one, look to Borgia. If you must be ruthless yet gracious, generous yet severe, if you have to wipe out a disloyal army and build a new one, and if you must maintain friendships with kings and princes so they eagerly help you and are terrified to cross you—you will never find a better, more perfect example than the actions of Cesare Borgia.

The only real mistake you can blame him for was his role in the election of Pope Julius the Second. He made a terrible choice. As I mentioned, even if he couldn't force his own candidate into the papacy, he had the veto power to block anyone else. He should never have allowed a cardinal he had previously injured, or one who had reason to fear him, to become Pope. Men will hurt you for one of two reasons: out of fear, or out of hatred.

The cardinals he had directly injured included San Pietro ad Vincula, Colonna, San Giorgio, and Ascanio. If any of the others had won, they would have feared him anyway, with the exception of the Cardinal of Rouen and the Spanish cardinals. The Spanish were tied to him through alliances and debt, and Rouen was backed by the immense power of the French Kingdom. Therefore, above all else, the Duke should have pushed a Spaniard into the papacy. If he couldn't do that, he should have backed Rouen. He absolutely never should have consented to San Pietro ad Vincula. Anyone who believes that handing out new favors will make powerful men forget old injuries is dangerously foolish. The Duke made a fatal error in this election, and it was the ultimate cause of his complete ruin.
